### #51 Component classes can silently collide with system.css - .res made rows 24px wide, .win hid the winning score

_opened · created 2026-08-11_

Two new component classes silently reused names `system.css` already defines. Both produced
broken layout with no error anywhere, and cost four rounds of review because the symptom looked
like a layout problem and the cause was a name.

## What happened

A "played match" variant of the shared match row was added, with a `res` modifier on the row and
a `win` modifier on the winning side's score.

| Class | What `system.css` already uses it for | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| `.res` | `system.css:155` — the **W/D/L result chip** in the `.rmatch` row: `width: 24px; height: 24px; display: grid; place-items: center` | every played row rendered **24 pixels wide** |
| `.win` | `system.css:93` — the **segment control's hidden panel**: `display: none` | the **winning side's score was invisible** |

At 24px the row's grid tracks resolved to `0px 41px`: the club name collapsed to nothing, the
kick-off overflowed on top of the badges, and consecutive rows overlapped. It looked exactly like
a flexbox/grid sizing bug.

⚠ **Nothing failed.** Not the build, not a linter, not the page-spec checker, not the existing
consistency checks — which compared the markup across surfaces and found it perfectly consistent,
because every surface was equally broken.

## Why it took four rounds

Every fix targeted the symptom: the score's alignment, the name's wrapping mode, the row's inner
layout, the kick-off's weight. None could have worked. The lesson is not "look harder" — it is
that **the wrong tool was being used**: the cause was found in under a minute once the row was
measured in a browser instead of reasoned about from the stylesheet.

⚠ The mocks could not be rendered at all: the browser pane cannot open `file://` URLs, so four
rounds ran on inference. Serving the folder over `http://127.0.0.1` fixed that instantly. **Any
future design review should measure, not read.**

## The guard

`check_row_consistency.py` now fails if a block emits any class that `system.css` already
defines, unless that class is on an explicit BORROWED list (the design-system components the
block is deliberately reusing: `fxrow`, `crest`, `nm`, …).

It caught `.win` within seconds of catching `.res` — a second live bug that had not been noticed.

## What this should become in the repo

The mock's guard protects the mocks. The same hazard exists in `site_v2/src/components/**`, where
every component writes class names into one global stylesheet.

**Recommendation — a naming rule, machine-checkable:** a component's own state/variant classes
must carry a prefix `system.css` never uses, e.g. `is-`. `is-played`, `is-winner`. Reuse of a
design-system class stays bare and therefore deliberate and visible.

The convention already exists in the tree: the tab bar's active state uses `.is-on`. This would
make it a rule rather than a coincidence, and the check is one grep — no `is-*` class may appear
in `system.css`, and any bare class a component introduces must already exist there.

⚠ **Not yet checked: whether any SHIPPED component already collides.** That sweep is the first
task on this issue, and it is a different question from the mocks — `system.css` is 507 lines of
shared vocabulary and nothing today stops a new component from landing on top of a name.

## Related

- **#50** — the "Next matches" block standard, which is what these classes belong to.
- ⚠ Do not touch `!27`.

### #52 Interaction standard: what is clickable, where the click boundary is, and how it signals - 9 element types, 6 hover treatments, no rule

_opened · created 2026-08-11_

**CPO, 2026-08-10:** *"mouse-over hover and then underlined club names is so 90s ... we need a
consistent approach as well: standardized where to click, which elements redirect where,
standardizing the elements etc."*

Nothing here is decided. This issue exists so the finding and the question are not lost.

## Measured, not remembered

Scanned across the four rendered surfaces (home, Matches next, Matches past, competition page):
**nine clickable element types, six different hover treatments, no rule connecting them.**

| What a reader clicks | n | Goes to | How it signals it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Match row | 46 | fixture | underlines the **club name** |
| Board row (Top players / Top teams) | 56 | player / team | underlines the name |
| Team row in the standings table | 18 | team | underlines the name |
| Competition heading | 15 | competition | underlines the name |
| Browse chip | 12 | competition | border colour + text colour |
| Tab | 4 | sibling page | text colour |
| Breadcrumb | 3 | home | underline |
| Nav item | — | (nothing yet) | text colour + background |
| Icon button | — | — | colour + border colour |

## Two problems, and the second is the worse one

1. **Six treatments for one idea.** Underline, colour, colour+background, border+colour, and two
   that do nothing.
2. **⚠ THE AFFORDANCE POINTS AT THE WRONG ELEMENT.** The whole match row is the link, but hover
   underlines the *club name* — and a row contains **two** club names. It tells a reader the name
   is the target when the target is the row. The same is true of the board row and the standings
   row.

## The shape of a rule (proposal only — not decided)

**The thing that responds is the thing you click.**

| Target | Affordance |
|---|---|
| A whole ROW | the row responds — a background lift to `--surface`, name to full `--ink`. No text decoration, no movement. |
| A CHIP or button | the chip responds — border and text colour. Already true. |
| A link in PROSE (the lede, a footnote) | keeps a real underline — in running text, colour alone is not an accessible signal. |
| A structural text link (heading, breadcrumb) | colour shift only, no underline. |

Plus two rules that are not about looks:

- **Never nest a link inside a link.** A row that is a link cannot contain a team link. Today the
  standings row and the match row both risk this as pages get wired.
- **One element, one destination.** If a row leads to the fixture, nothing inside it may lead
  somewhere else — that ambiguity is what the underline is currently creating.

⚠ **Keyboard focus is a separate signal and must survive whatever is chosen.** `system.css`
already has a focus-visible rule; a decision that only changes `:hover` leaves it intact, but a
decision that removes the underline everywhere must not remove it from focus.

## Where this connects

- **#50** — the "Next matches" block standard defines the row; this defines what the row *does*.
- **#45** — internal linking owns *which* page each element targets. This issue owns *how it
  signals* and *where the click boundary is*, not the destinations.
- **#48** — the nav items have hover states and no destinations at all.

## Not yet answered

- Does a row lift on hover, or is a border/edge treatment preferred?
- Do structural text links keep any underline at all, or colour only?
- What happens on touch, where there is no hover? (Today: nothing signals anything.)
- Is the whole row clickable on a phone, or does that make scroll-tapping error-prone?

⚠ Do not touch `!27`.

### #53 Nightly prod build FAILS: 10 Macau events mis-attributed to Mação (Portugal) breaks assert_event_team_in_fixture_participants

_opened · created 2026-08-11_

## The nightly prod build is failing, and it will fail again at 04:00 tonight

`assert_event_team_in_fixture_participants` FAILED on the 2026-08-11 04:00 nightly
(`fdp-nightly-xz4w9`, exit 1): **Got 10 results, configured to fail if != 0**.

Because `dbt build` halts on error, **540 of 970 nodes were SKIPPED**. Raw data is current;
`dbt_analytics` did NOT fully rebuild this morning. This recurs every night until it is fixed.

    Done. PASS=428 WARN=1 ERROR=1 SKIP=540 TOTAL=970

### NOT caused by the recent merges

The same test passed on the 2026-08-10 run (`PASS=969 WARN=1 ERROR=0`) on the SAME image
(`sha256:0955e004`), which already contained items 8a and 8b. Nothing about the write-mode or
cadence work touches fixture events. This is newly-ingested data tripping an existing guard —
which is the guard doing its job.

### The 10 rows are one team in one two-legged tie

| league | fixture_sk | events | event team_sk | home | away |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| WCQAS | 1100381 | 7 | **4767** | 1556 | 1544 |
| WCQAS | 1100382 | 3 | **4767** | 1544 | 1556 |

Two fixtures, same two nations home-and-away. Every violating event names the same third team.

    team_sk  team_api_id  team_name  team_country
    1544     1544         Macau      (null)
    1556     1556         Myanmar    Myanmar
    4767     4767         Mação      Portugal

**Mação is a Portuguese municipality. Macau is the AFC territory.** A Portuguese team cannot
appear in WC Qualifiers Asia. API-Football has attributed Macau's events to a similarly-named
Portuguese entity — a name-collision mis-attribution, the exact class #526 built this guard for.

### The evidence that settles which team the events belong to

    Mação (4767) fixtures as a participant : 0
    Mação (4767) fixtures with events      : 2   <- only these two
    Macau (1544) fixtures as a participant : 2   <- the same two

Mação exists in `dim_team` **only as an attribution artefact** — it never plays anything in our
data. Macau plays exactly the two fixtures whose events are mis-tagged. The events belong to
Macau.

### Recommended fix — the mechanism already exists

`dbt_project/seeds/fixture_event_team_overrides.csv`, which already carries two corrections of
this class:

    wrong_team_api_id,correct_team_api_id,mode,note
    2263,10124,alias,Riga FC duplicate provider id 2263 -> canonical 10124 (#526)
    6424,25274,reattribute_if_cohabiting,ASKO Kara 25274 events mis-tagged to rival ASC Kara 6424 in CAFCL 2020-24 (#526)

Proposed row:

    4767,1544,reattribute_if_cohabiting,Macau 1544 events mis-tagged to Mação 4767 (Portuguese municipality, name collision) in WCQAS fixtures 1100381/1100382

**`reattribute_if_cohabiting`, NOT `alias`.** Mação and Macau are genuinely different real-world
entities; they are not one club under two provider ids. `alias` would permanently conflate them,
so if Mação ever legitimately appears in Portuguese football it would be silently merged into a
national team. `reattribute_if_cohabiting` corrects the events only in fixtures where Macau
actually participates, which is precisely the ASKO Kara precedent.

⚠ NOT APPLIED. The override seed is configuration governed by the CPO, and this is an
entity-identity call — the repo's standing rule is to verify identity against EXTERNAL ground
truth before asserting two records relate. The external facts here are that Mação is a
municipality in Portugal and Macau is an AFC member; both are checkable, and both are stated
above so the ruling can be made on evidence rather than on my inference.

### Until it is fixed

Every nightly errors and skips ~540 nodes, so the warehouse stays stale even though ingestion
succeeds. Two options, both CPO calls:

1. **Apply the override row** (recommended) — corrects the data at source-of-truth and the test
   goes green.
2. Leave it and accept a red nightly until the provider corrects its data, in which case the
   `fdp-nightly execution failed` alert fires nightly and will be tuned out. Not recommended for
   that reason.

### Footnote: the monitoring worked

This is the first genuinely unattended failure since #39, and it was detected rather than
discovered by accident. The `run.googleapis.com/job/completed_execution_count{result=failed}`
metric registered at 05:29Z and the `fdp-nightly execution failed` policy fired. That is the
alerting doing exactly what it was built for, on a real failure rather than a manufactured one.

Refs #526, #546

### #58 Every page design must declare where each element's data comes from - no hard-coded content, and a value with no source is a named gap

_opened · created 2026-08-11_

**CPO, 2026-08-10:** *"While we are working on the pages that put the whole website together, we
need to clarify where the data come from that populate the content. I want the content as much
data-backed as possible without any hard-coding. Your mockups always follow some instinct without
clarifying where the data come from."*

Correct, and it was the pattern of a whole day's design session rather than a single lapse.

## The evidence

Every one of these was typed into a mock on instinct and only justified when the CPO asked where
it came from:

| Typed value | Where it should have come from | How it was caught |
|---|---|---|
| Browse headings *"Europe / North & Central America / Asia"* | nowhere — **both the labels and the grouping axis were invented**; `site_architecture.md` §4 documents two axes and confederation is neither | *"Where does the grouping come from? Is it data backed or hard-coded in the mock?"* |
| The seven category names | `competition_types.csv` (#57) | *"the single source of truth for the displayed name is this seed file"* |
| Short competition names | `dim_league.league_name` (#55) | *"1. Fussball-Bundesliga is just Bundesliga"* |
| Venue-local timezones | derivable from the registry's `country`; still typed | asked directly |
| The "active twelve" filter | **the export applies no status filter at all** — the assumption was invented | *"some of them are already onboarded btw"* |
| *"Top flight"* on every row | a `tier` field that says almost nothing | *"top flight top tier drop"* |
| The continent on a competition row | registry `country`, which is a country OR a continent OR `"International"`, inconsistently | *"Where does the continent assignment come from?"* |

⚠ **The through-line is not that the values were wrong.** Several were right. It is that the SOURCE
was never stated, so nobody could tell a real field from a guess without interrogating each one.

⚠ **The pattern already had a fix and it was not reused.** The "Next matches" block standard
(**#50**) carries an ANATOMY table naming the column behind every element on the block. That was
built once, worked, and was then not applied to any subsequent page.

## The rule

**Every page design declares, per element, where its data comes from. Anything with no source is a
named gap, never a typed value.**

Concretely, a page design is not reviewable until it carries a provenance table of the same shape
as #50's:

| Element | Level | Source | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Competition name | heading | `dim_league.league_name` | one source; today there are two (#55) |
| Category | heading | `seeds/competition_types.csv` → `label_en` | |
| Kick-off | row | `fct_fixture.kickoff_datetime` | |
| Timezone | row | ⚠ **not derivable yet** | flagged, not filled |

And three rules that follow from it:

1. **A value with no source is a GAP, and it is named as one.** It may be stubbed to render the
   mock, but it must be visibly marked and it must be guarded so it cannot silently drift from
   whatever real set it stands in for.
2. **A stub is guarded.** Every stand-in used today (`SHORT_NAME`, `ZONE`, the proposed seed) has
   a guard that fails if it diverges from the registry or the shipped seed. That is the minimum,
   not a nicety — it is what stops a mock being designed against data that does not exist.
3. **Do not invent a category, an axis or a grouping.** If the model does not carry it, it is not
   a design decision to make in a mock; it is a data-model change to propose.

## Where it should live

The mechanism already exists — this is a rule, not a new machine:

- `site_v2/src/specs/**/*.spec.json` already declares each page's blocks and each block's backing
  mart, and `check-page-specs.mjs` already fails the build when a named source does not exist.
  ⚠ It checks that the source EXISTS; it does not check that every rendered element HAS one.
- `page-spec.schema.json` documents the shape and would carry the addition.

So the ask is a per-element provenance declaration alongside the existing per-block one, and the
checker extended to fail on an element with no declared source.

⚠ **Scope check before building anything:** every page designed today would need this filled in —
the competitions page (#54), the competition page (#47), the Matches pages (#50), the interaction
standard (#52 — no data, so trivially none). Doing that retrospectively is the test of whether the
rule is workable.

## Related

- **#50** the block standard, which already does this correctly and is the model to copy
- **#55** competition display names · **#57** the taxonomy seed · **#54** the competitions page
- ⚠ Do not touch `!27`.

### #59 Commit gate validates the wrong repository in a worktree session (fail-open)

_opened · created 2026-08-11_

## The commit gate validates the wrong repository in a worktree session

**This is a fail-OPEN hole, not just an inconvenience.** In a worktree session the governance
gate reads another directory's artifacts, so a genuinely failing review can be waved through by an
unrelated clean `review.md`.

### Mechanism

`.claude/settings.json:30` registers the gate as:

    python "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claude/hooks/git_discipline.py"

and `git_discipline.py:90-91` resolves its root as:

    def _repo_root() -> str:
        return os.environ.get("CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR") or os.getcwd()

`CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` is the directory the session was LAUNCHED from, not the directory the work is
in. So when a session launched from `D:\Projects\football-data-pipeline` does its work in the
`fdp-pipeline` worktree, **both** the hook file that executes **and** every artifact it validates
come from the launch directory:

- `review.md` — read from the wrong worktree (`git_discipline.py:651`)
- the staged diff the `diff_sha256` is checked against (`_staged_diff_bytes(root)`)
- `review_routing.json`, `contract.md`, and the `--staged-hash` / `--review-patch` CLI modes

### Observed, 2026-08-08

A commit in `fdp-pipeline` was refused with "a reviewer verdict is FAIL". The branch's own
`review.md` contained zero `VERDICT: FAIL`; the PARKED clone's contained two, belonging to an
unrelated branch. The hash check passed *before* that, which only makes sense if it had compared
the parked clone's staged diff against the parked clone's `review.md` — i.e. the gate was
operating entirely on a different repository.

### Why the other direction is worse

That instance failed closed by luck. Reverse it — a clean `review.md` in the launch directory,
a failing review in the worktree — and the commit sails through. The same applies to the hash
binding: `diff_sha256` would be checked against the wrong staged diff entirely.

Also worth noting: the hook file that runs is the launch directory's copy. If that clone has
uncommitted changes to `git_discipline.py` (it did — 149 lines ahead of `main` on an unmerged
branch), then **every worktree session is governed by another stream's work-in-progress guard.**

### Not a theoretical concern

Three worktrees are in use today (`git worktree list`): the original clone plus `fdp-pipeline` and
`fdp-product`. Any session not launched from the directory it works in is affected.

### Suggested fix

Resolve the root from the hook event rather than the environment. Claude Code delivers the event
as JSON on stdin (`_command_utils.read_event()`), and it carries the session's real `cwd`. Prefer
that when it resolves inside a git repository; fall back to `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, then
`os.getcwd()`. The two CLI modes (`--staged-hash`, `--review-patch`) have no event and should keep
using the current behaviour — or better, `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` from the caller's cwd.

Pin it with a test that runs the gate with `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` pointing at a different repo than
the event's `cwd`, and asserts the verdict comes from the event's repo. Without that, the fix is
untestable in exactly the configuration it exists for.

### Constraints on doing it

`.claude/hooks/**` is a PROTECTED path: needs a CPO-approved governance task carrying
`protected_override` and a non-placeholder `impact_map`, and routes to `cto-reviewer` +
`platform-reviewer` at the opus floor.

**Do not attempt it while another stream has uncommitted changes in that file.** Two streams
editing the one file that governs every commit is how a bad merge lands in the worst possible
place. Check `git status .claude/hooks/git_discipline.py` in every worktree first.

### Workaround until then

Launch the session from the directory the work is in. That makes `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` correct and
everything resolves properly, with no code change. It is a discipline, not a guard — nothing
enforces it, which is why the fix is still worth doing.

### #60 Worktree layout: the canonical clone is parked on a feature branch and every default points at it

_opened · created 2026-08-11_

## Worktree layout: the canonical clone is parked on a feature branch, and everything defaults to it

Three directories serve one repository. The problem is not the count — it is that **the one every
default points at is the one nobody works in, and it is neither clean nor on `main`.**

    git worktree list      (2026-08-11)
    D:/Projects/football-data-pipeline  6352d7d  [fix/20-push-judged-by-target]   <- parked, dirty
    D:/Projects/fdp-pipeline            c742b96  [main]
    D:/Projects/fdp-product             0937412  [feat/367-landing-page]

`football-data-pipeline` is the original clone. It is 60+ commits behind `main`, sits on an
unmerged feature branch, and carries uncommitted work — including `.claude/hooks/git_discipline.py`,
149 lines ahead of `main`. Yet it is what `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` points at for any session launched
there, which makes it the source of truth for hooks and `.claude/task/*` regardless of where the
work happens.

### What this actually caused, in one session

- The commit gate read the parked clone's `review.md` and refused a commit on another branch's
  stale verdicts. Filed separately — that one is a fail-open hole and needs a code fix.
- The agent's shell started in the parked clone on every call, and `cd` does not persist, so
  `git commit` — which must be the sole command in its call — had no legal spelling from the
  worktree. Three MRs were committed by hand as a result.
- The local `main` ref went stale twice, silently making `--review-patch` re-include
  already-merged work. Caught both times only by eyeballing the file count in the patch.
- Every stash operation had to be matched by message rather than index, because the stash stack is
  shared across all three worktrees and holds 14 entries of load-bearing WIP from other streams.

None of these are hard problems individually. Together they cost most of a session.

### Suggested cleanup, cheapest first

1. **Land or properly park the WIP in `football-data-pipeline`** — the hook changes above all.
   Uncommitted work in a parked directory currently governs two other streams.
2. **Put that clone on `main` and leave it there.** It becomes a stable anchor whose defaults are
   never wrong. Feature work lives in worktrees; the anchor never carries a feature branch.
3. **Make the names consistent.** One directory is `football-data-pipeline`, two are `fdp-*`,
   which reads like separate repositories. Either `fdp-main` / `fdp-pipeline` / `fdp-product`, or
   drop the prefix everywhere. Cosmetic, but it is what makes the layout legible at a glance.
4. **Write the convention down** — one line in `CLAUDE.md`: which directory is the anchor, that it
   stays on `main`, and that a session is launched from the worktree it works in. Right now that
   knowledge exists only in whoever set it up.

### Related

- The hook/worktree governance hole is filed separately and is the only part of this that needs a
  code change; everything above is housekeeping.
- The shared stash stack is inherent to git worktrees, not a defect. Worth a note in `CLAUDE.md`
  alongside the existing warning, since 14 entries deep it is genuinely hazardous: always
  `git stash push -m "<unique-tag>"` and pop by matching the message, never by index.

### #61 deploy/nightly README alert-policy loop deploys only 2 of 3 declared policies

_opened · created 2026-08-11_

Found on 2026-08-11 while doing #33 "delete the 25h bridge policy".

## What was wrong in production

`deploy/nightly/alert-policy.json` declares **three** policies. Only **two** were live:

    LIVE     fdp raw data is STALE or uncheckable
    MISSING  fdp freshness sentinel itself stopped     <- the watcher-of-the-watcher
    LIVE     fdp-nightly execution failed

`fdp freshness sentinel itself stopped` has now been deployed
(`alertPolicies/751471063453009885`, enabled, absent_for 3h, same email channel), and the
25h bridge policy has been deleted. Live state now matches the JSON.

## Why it happened — the recipe under-deploys

`deploy/nightly/README.md` (the "Create the alert policies" section) ends with:

    for i in 0 1; do
      curl ... -d @pol$i.json
    done
    rm -f pol0.json pol1.json

The index list is **hardcoded to two** while the generator loop above it writes one file per
declared policy. The file has since grown to three, so index 2 is written and never POSTed,
and `rm` leaves it behind. The prose one line above still says "alert-policy.json holds BOTH
policies", which is also stale.

This is the "fix the class, not the instance" shape: a hardcoded list that silently stops
covering the thing it enumerates. It fails OPEN — the missing policy is the one that detects
the monitoring itself having stopped, so the gap is invisible by construction.

## Why it mattered here

`fdp-freshness` runs the SAME IMAGE as `fdp-nightly`. One bad image deploy takes out both
jobs. With the watcher missing AND the 25h bridge deleted, that scenario would have raised no
alert at all — the six-day silent-outage class #39 exists to close. The bridge was therefore
deployed-then-deleted in that order rather than deleted first (CPO decision, 2026-08-11).

## Suggested fix

1. Derive the loop from the file instead of hardcoding: iterate over the generated `pol*.json`
   rather than `0 1`, and clean up the same way.
2. Correct "holds BOTH policies" to say the count is whatever the file declares.
3. Consider making the apply step genuinely idempotent — the README already warns that neither
   POST has an existence check, and a duplicate means every alert arrives twice. A read-then-
   PATCH-or-POST keyed on `displayName` removes the warning rather than documenting it.

Note `deploy/nightly/README.md` is not a protected path, but this is a mechanism change to the
deploy recipe, so it wants its own task contract and a platform review.

Refs #39, #33

### #63 Review-binding hash is computed over rendered diff text, so local and CI disagree - blocks every MR

_closed · created 2026-08-12 · closed 2026-08-14_

`validate:governance` fails on **!33** and will fail on **every merge request after it**, because
the review-binding hash is computed over a *presentation format* rather than over content.

## What happens

`review.md` carries a `diff_sha256` that binds the review to the code being merged. The local
commit gate computes it; `scripts/check_task_artifacts.py` recomputes it in CI and refuses the
build if they differ. On !33 they differ:

```
local  : 0c1ef8aff9aca4eb7902911b41b380c12c10f82e43c8855ac7f774af23cfd517
CI     : be3a493dfe912eadad79f52f4572b1bf1f57c5ce373c6dbc2820a5ec1ae9838a
```

## What it is NOT — each ruled out by measurement, not by reasoning

| checked | result |
|---|---|
| different commits on the two sides | **no** — `git ls-remote` confirms remote branch and remote `main` match local exactly |
| the base it diffs against | **no** — five candidate bases tested locally, none reproduces CI's number |
| the number of commits on the branch | **no** — CI produced the SAME hash for two different versions of the branch |
| line endings | **no** — the diff contains **zero** CR bytes; neither CRLF→LF nor LF→CRLF reproduces CI's number |
| local `diff.*` git config | **no** — defaults everywhere, nothing that alters rendering |

⚠ **And it has never worked here.** !33 is the FIRST merge request to actually reach this check —
`main`'s own pipeline and !34 both died on `ci_quota_exceeded` before running it. So this is not a
regression; it is a latent defect the new self-hosted runner has exposed by letting the check run
at all.

## Root cause

Both sides hash **the rendered patch text** — the human-readable output of `git diff`. That is a
presentation format: its bytes depend on git version, platform and diff settings. Hashing it means
the same code can produce two different hashes on two machines.

**Demonstrable on one machine**, identical commits, only a display setting changed:

```
rendered, -U3   ->  0c1ef8af…   51,628 bytes
rendered, -U0   ->  ca1afb7d…   46,687 bytes   <- same content, different hash
--raw           ->  974cd829…    1,459 bytes   <- content identity, stable
```

## Fix

Hash **content identity** instead: `git diff --raw`, which emits
`:mode mode <blobA> <blobB> STATUS<TAB>path`. Blob SHAs are content hashes — identical on every
platform and git version. Same guarantee the check exists to provide, none of the fragility, and
1,459 bytes instead of 51,628.

⚠ **Two implementations must change together** or local and CI diverge permanently:
`.claude/hooks/git_discipline.py::_staged_diff_bytes` (feeds the commit gate and `--staged-hash`)
and `scripts/check_task_artifacts.py` (the CI recompute).

## Second defect, same family, worth fixing in the same change

`_staged_diff_bytes` diffs `--staged` (HEAD→index) while CI diffs `base...HEAD`. On a **multi-commit
branch those are different diffs**, so the local number is simply wrong — which is why `CLAUDE.md`
carries a standing warning that `--staged-hash` is "the WRONG number" on a second commit. It cost
two wasted cycles on !33 alone. `_review_patch_bytes` already resolves the base correctly via
`_cumulative_diff` / `_base_commit`; reuse that rather than writing a second resolver, and delete
the CLAUDE.md warning rather than qualifying it.

## Tests

The existing `test_local_staged_hash_equals_ci_recompute` cannot catch this — it runs both sides on
one machine with one git, so it is green against the defect. Needed:

- an **invariance** test: the same content hashed with different rendering settings must produce
  the same hash. Written so it FAILS against today's implementation (it does).
- a **multi-commit** test: local `--staged-hash` must equal the CI recompute after two commits.
  Also fails today.

## Consequence to plan for

Changing the algorithm **invalidates every existing `review.md` hash**. Both open MRs — !27 and
!33 — need rebinding after this merges.

## Governance

`.claude/hooks/` is a PROTECTED prefix, so this needs `protected_override` with CPO authority, an
impact_map, and cto-reviewer + platform-reviewer at the opus floor.

⚠ This blocks !33 and !27. It should merge first.

### #64 #63 residuals: four unpinned or imprecise spots the review rounds declined to expand into

_opened · created 2026-08-13_

Four residuals recorded by **platform-reviewer (opus)** and **cto-reviewer (opus)** during #63's four
review rounds, each explicitly judged **not grounds for another round** and filed here so they are
not rediscovered as new. None is a bypass; the two behavioural ones fail CLOSED (a false rejection,
never a false pass).

## 1. Two `_base_commit` raise paths have no test

`.claude/hooks/git_discipline.py:435` — the new "`GOVERNANCE_BASE` resolves but shares no history
with HEAD" raise, and the identical pre-existing one at `:458` for the ref loop.

Their CONSEQUENCE is pinned (`test_commit_gate_denies_when_the_hash_cannot_be_computed` covers
deny + exit 1); only the trigger condition is unpinned, and reaching it needs a two-root repository
fixture. Worth adding because #63 itself was a lesson in unpinned branches — three tests in that
task passed either way until they were run against a reverted copy.

## 2. The override test compares against a locally-built command, not the CI-shaped one

`tests/test_governance_hooks.py:1910-1914` builds `git diff --staged <merge-base>` itself rather
than calling `branch_hash(ci_repo, base="upstream")` after a commit.

One line stronger, and it would cover the only residual divergence platform-reviewer could
construct: a **criss-cross history with multiple merge bases**, where `git merge-base HEAD <ref>`
and `<ref>...HEAD` need not agree. ⚠ That failure mode is a false REJECTION — fail-closed, never a
bypass.

## 3. Tests inherit an ambient `GOVERNANCE_BASE`

`tests/test_governance_hooks.py:1014`, and the direct hook runs at `:1901` and `:1941`.

The deny message actively tells operators to export that variable, so a developer who follows the
instruction and leaves it exported would make
`test_base_resolution_prefers_the_remote_tracking_ref_over_a_stale_local_main` pass **without ever
exercising the preference loop**. Same class as the `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` fragility already fixed in
#63 round 3. CI does not set it, so this is developer-machine only.

## 4. Deny-message and doc precision for the unrelated-histories case

`.claude/hooks/git_discipline.py:435-439` and `:162-168`, plus `contract.md:130` and
`docs/agent_guardrails.md`, all describe the remedy as *"fetch the base branch, or set
`GOVERNANCE_BASE`"*.

After #63's round-4 change that is underspecified for the two-histories-with-no-common-ancestor
case: setting the variable to the base branch now denies a second time, and only a commit **in
HEAD's own ancestry** works. An exit exists — cto-reviewer confirmed
`git rev-list --max-parents=0 HEAD` reaches it — but no message names it.

## Also noted, PRE-EXISTING and not caused by #63

`git_discipline.py:137-146` derives the required-reviewer set from `--staged` (HEAD-vs-index) while
the hash it checks is cumulative from the base. On a multi-commit branch the LOCAL gate can
therefore require fewer reviewers than CI, which enumerates paths cumulatively.

⚠ CI is the stricter side and fails closed, so nothing reaches `main` under-reviewed — but the two
halves disagreeing about which reviewers a branch needs is the same class of local/CI split that
#63 existed to remove, and it is worth closing deliberately rather than leaving as an accident.

## Related

**#63** (the review-binding hash), and its four review rounds — the findings above are the residue
those rounds explicitly declined to expand into.

### #65 data:build:mr fails on a stale worktree registration left by the previous job

_closed · created 2026-08-13 · closed 2026-08-14 · labels: bug_

CI job `data:build:mr` fails at:

```
git worktree add --detach /tmp/main-src FETCH_HEAD
fatal: /tmp/main-src is a missing but already registered worktree
ERROR: Job failed: exit code 128
```

`.gitlab-ci.yml:555`.

## Cause, verified from two job logs

The self-hosted runner (`ci-runner-01`) persists the **project directory** between jobs but gives each job a **fresh `/tmp`**. `git worktree add` writes its registration into the persisted `.git/worktrees/`, so after the first run the registration outlives the directory it points at.

- Job 15864168006 (2026-08-12): `Preparing worktree (detached HEAD a2b4184e)` — **succeeded**, registering `/tmp/main-src`.
- Job on pipeline 2756651714 (2026-08-13): same command, **exit 128**, registration present, directory gone.

This is a consequence of the runner migration. On the previous shared runners every job got a clean clone, so the registration never survived. It will now fail on **every** MR that matches `data_paths_mr`.

## Fix

`git worktree prune` before the `add`. Prune drops registrations whose directories are gone and is a no-op otherwise. `git worktree add -f` also silences it but overrides a *live* worktree too, which hides the real condition instead of clearing it.

## Not this issue

The `assert_event_team_in_fixture_participants` failure seen further down the same job on 08-12 is separate — see the sibling issue.

### #66 Prod data is stale since 2026-08-09; #53 merged but was never applied

_closed · created 2026-08-13 · closed 2026-08-13 · labels: bug_

Prod BigQuery data has not been rebuilt since **2026-08-09 08:38** (`data:nightly=success` at `8ac63f65`). Every data job on `main` since then failed with `failure_reason: ci_quota_exceeded`:

| `a2b4184e`, `b4b2414a` | 08-12, 08-13 | — | no data job (paths did not match) |

## Consequence

**#53 is merged but has never reached prod.** `fixture_event_team_overrides.csv` carries the Macau correction (`4767 -> 1544`), but prod `fct_fixture_event` predates it, so the singular DQ test still fails:

Ten — exactly the count #53 named. On an MR, `dbt build --select state:modified+` rebuilds only modified models and `--defer --favor-state` resolves the rest to **prod**, so this test reads prod and will stay red on every MR until prod is rebuilt. The same applies to #61.

Blocked behind #65 for the MR path only; the `main` path does not use the worktree step.

Related: there is still **no nightly schedule on GitLab**, so nothing refreshes this on a timer — also a recurring-cost decision.

### #69 Countries are free text in four dims with no mapping table, no dim and no tests

_opened · created 2026-08-14 · labels: bug_

**CPO ruling, 2026-08-14:** *"Our transformation layer is the place where we clean, reconcile and
standardize the data. We can even impute missing information after researching properly… We don't
need to accept this. Raw doesn't define the taxonomies or categories or whatever. We do it in a way
that makes sense for our purpose."* And, on separating countries from continents with a boolean
flag: *"that is bullshit… I'd assume that these entries are somewhere in a mapping table and/or then
a dim table if we use them for a mart."*

Correct on both counts. This issue is the consequence.

## What is actually there today

**Country is free text in at least four places, and nothing reconciles them:**

| where | column | tests |
|---|---|---|
| `dim_league` | `league_country`, `country_flag_url` | **none** (`core.yml` says `tests: None`) |
| `dim_team` | `team_country` | none |
| `dim_player` | `player_birth_country` | none |
| `dim_coach` | `coach_birth_country` | none |

All provider-sourced (`stg_apif__leagues.sql:53` pulls `$.league.country` and `$.league.flag`).
There is **no countries seed, no `dim_country`, and no mapping table** — `dbt_project/seeds/` holds
`competition_registry`, `competition_types`, `confederations`, `fixture_event_team_overrides`,
`metric_catalogue`, `team_name_overrides`, `wc_team_market_value_snapshot` and nothing else.

**And `docs/competition_registry.yml` carries a SECOND, hand-typed copy** whose values are not
countries at all for 24 of 45 competitions: `Africa`, `Asia`, `Europe`, `International`,
`North/Central America`, `South America`. It was going to be projected into the warehouse as part of
#62 step 1; that is now cancelled, because it would have made a third copy.

## The shape

Same pattern as `confederations.csv` (#57):

```
countries.csv    country_key, label_i18n_key, label_en, confederation
dim_country      published from the seed

dim_league.league_country     -> FK -> dim_country
dim_team.team_country         -> FK -> dim_country
dim_player.player_birth_country -> FK -> dim_country
dim_coach.coach_birth_country   -> FK -> dim_country
```

Under this, `Europe` and `International` cannot enter a country column — they fail the foreign key.
No rule to remember, no flag to check, no reviewer needed to notice.

Per the 2026-08-14 refinement on #62: the seed carries the **key** and the **English name**;
translations live in the i18n surface keyed off `label_i18n_key`.

## Order of work

1. ⚠ **DISCOVERY FIRST — do not author the list from memory.** Nobody knows what values exist.
   `bq query --dry_run` to price a `SELECT DISTINCT` per surface (free, exact bytes), then run it.
   ⚠ `dim_player` is ~154k rows, so price before running.
2. The canonical list and the English names go to the CPO. **Names are copy and therefore his
   (§10)** — do not settle "South Korea" vs "Korea Republic" unilaterally.
3. Seed + `dim_country`.
4. Wire the FKs **one surface at a time**, each with its reconciliation recorded.
   ⚠ **Expect failure on first contact, and that is the point.** Provider values will not match a
   clean list — "World" for international competitions, spelling and abbreviation differences. Fix
   by mapping, never by loosening the test (`feedback_never_loosen_a_guard`).
5. Decide what happens to the registry's `country` field once the export no longer reads the YAML
   (#62 step 4). Blanking the 24 non-country values there today would change what the site renders,
   because `export_site_data.py:911` still reads it directly.

## Why it is not folded into #62 step 1

Step 1 projects five registry-owned columns (`confederation`, `slug`, `sort_order`, `tier`,
`season_type`) that nothing else has. It is small and self-contained. This is a new entity touching
four dims with a DQ gate that will legitimately go red until reconciled — different files, different
risk. Step 1 does not touch country and is not blocked by this.

## Related

- **#62** one mart per page block — where this surfaced
- **#57** `confederations.csv`, the pattern this copies
- **#55** display name single source · **#850/#851** provider name = display AND identity, the same
  class of problem for teams

### #70 Scan-budget guard: fail CI when a change makes each competition more expensive (#33 item 11)

_opened · created 2026-08-14_

Parked deliberately on 2026-08-14 to move to product work. Filed so it is not lost.

## The problem it solves

**Nothing tells us a change made the pipeline more expensive.** We find out from the bill, weeks
later. That has happened twice already:

- A cost fix landed 2026-05-25 and an unrelated refactor reverted it two days later. Invisible
  for TWO MONTHS, because all ~865 dbt tests ask whether a NUMBER is correct and none asks
  whether something became expensive. That is why `tests/test_materialisation_policy.py` exists.
- `1_staging` sat as a view re-scanning raw JSON for the entire life of the project, until
  measured on 2026-08-12 (#33 items 9/10).

## How it works

BigQuery reports `total_bytes_processed` for a **dry run** (`dry_run=True`,
`use_query_cache=False`). Dry runs are FREE and execute nothing. So: `dbt compile --target prod`,
submit every compiled model and test as a dry run, sum the bytes, compare against
`docs/scan_budget.yml`.

⭐ **THE BUDGET HOLDS TWO NUMBERS, and the second is the point:**

    total_gib_per_full_build
    gib_per_competition

A change that costs more because more competitions arrived PASSES. A change that makes **each
competition** more expensive FAILS. That distinction is the whole value, because cost here scales
with competitions and more are coming (CPO, 2026-08-12).

## ⚠ TWO CORRECTIONS TO #33 ITEM 11, both found before starting

**1. IT CANNOT LIVE IN `validate:governance`, which is what #33 specifies.** That job is purely
offline: no GCP credentials, no dbt, 42 seconds (verified 2026-08-14, `.gitlab-ci.yml:307-318` —
it runs only `check_layer_contract`, `check_registry_var_sync`, `check_competition_type_seed`,
`check_copy_gate`, `check_task_artifacts`). Wiring the guard there would give a fast offline gate
production credentials and a dbt compile, turning 42s into minutes and widening what holds prod
access.

**The right home is `data:build:mr`**, which already authenticates via WIF and already compiles.

**2. THEREFORE IT EDITS `.gitlab-ci.yml`, A PROTECTED PATH.** This is NOT the ~50-line drive-by
#33 implies. It needs a governance task with `protected_override`, a non-placeholder
`impact_map`, and BOTH `cto-reviewer` and `platform-reviewer` at the opus floor. Small in code,
large in process. Budget accordingly.

## Known caveat, stated up front

A dry run does not model clustering pruning, so it OVERESTIMATES. The guard therefore errs
toward failing when nothing is wrong, never toward silently passing. That is the safe direction,
but expect occasional false alarms and design the failure message to make the next step obvious.

## Baseline to record when built

Measured 2026-08-14, post items 8b/9/14/15:

    prod build, 24h:  tests $0.17  vs  models $0.07
    raw storage:      3.40 GiB (was 11.9 GiB before the merge-on-write and /injuries work)

Reproduce with `python scripts/report_bq_cost.py --days 1`.

## Dependencies

None. `google-cloud-bigquery` is already required, WIF is already in place, no new IAM.

Refs #33 item 11.

### #71 Stale-claim check: a correction lands in one artifact and the superseded claim survives in another

_opened · created 2026-08-14 · labels: bug_

**CPO, 2026-08-14:** *"it doesn't prevent you from doing the same mistakes anyway every time"* — said
of writing the lesson to memory. Correct, and the repo has already measured it: **#30 found 33 of 50
recorded corrections were prose only, 22 recurred, and every rule that got a mechanism stopped
recurring.** So this issue is the mechanism, not another note.

The unfiled "contract-claims-vs-tree check" that `.claude/active_work.md` has carried for weeks —
and that #30's own evidence ranked ABOVE the hook telemetry it put first — is this.

## The defect class, measured on 2026-08-14 alone

A design changes mid-task. I correct the artifact I am looking at. The superseded claim survives in
another file, **restated in different words**, so the grep I run does not find it. It is then caught
by a reviewer, never by me. Four occurrences in one session:

| # | superseded claim | corrected in | survived in | cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | "the column list is duplicated, a parity test makes it safe" | `check_registry_var_sync.py` | `sync_dbt_vars.py` comment | 1 round |
| 2 | same | 3 artifacts | the test's module docstring | 1 round |
| 3 | "these fields are consumed by the export ONLY, not by dbt" | seed schema | `docs/competition_registry.yml` header | 1 round |
| 4 | "NO REVIEW ROUND IS RUN" | `contract.md` | `review.md` | 2 rounds |

Five review rounds, all spent re-finding the same class. #3 is the worst of them: the false claim
sat in the file `.claude/skills/onboard-competition` sources its field table from, so an onboarder
would read "not by dbt" immediately before setting a field dbt now tests.

## Why a literal grep does not catch it

Because the restatement is a paraphrase. After #62's fix, `grep "Duplicated rather than imported"`
returned nothing while the test docstring said *"each declares its own `SEED_COLUMNS` because
neither import form works in both execution contexts"* — same dead claim, no shared phrase. The
sweep that eventually worked was `duplicat|each declares|its own SEED_COLUMNS|two lists|hand-copie|
restat` — the CONCEPT, not the sentence.

## Proposed check

`scripts/check_contract_claims.py`, wired into `validate:governance`. Two properties, both cheap and
both mechanical — no semantic matching:

**1. Cross-artifact contradiction on the task's own vocabulary.** For each `decisions_taken` item in
`contract.md`, extract its distinctive identifiers (backticked symbols, file paths, issue numbers).
For every identifier, find every OTHER artifact in the branch diff that mentions it. Emit them as a
REVIEW SURFACE — not a pass/fail, a list the builder must have read. Rationale: the tool cannot know
which claim is stale, but it can guarantee the builder is shown every file that talks about the
thing being changed. All four failures above were files that mentioned the identifier and were never
opened.

**2. Hard-fail on a claim that the tree contradicts.** Narrow and checkable, so it stays honest:
- a `contract.md` or `review.md` claim of the form "X is not in Y" / "Y does not contain X" where
  the tree shows otherwise
- a `docs/**` comment asserting a field is "not used by dbt" while the field appears in
  `dbt_project/seeds/schema.yml`
- a `rounds:` count in `review.md` that disagrees with the number of `VERDICT:` blocks recorded

⚠ Start with (1). It is the one that would have caught all four, and it cannot produce a false
accusation because it accuses nothing — it surfaces.

## Explicitly not this issue

Semantic similarity, an LLM reviewer, or anything that guesses which of two statements is true.
#26 already tried a keyword matcher for a related class and it was WITHDRAWN because a false hit
fires on a real rule. The value here is *coverage of what to re-read*, not a verdict.

## Related

- **#30** the audit finding that ranked this above hook telemetry, and the 33/50/22 measurement
- **#20** the other surviving BUILD item from that stream
- **#873** a matcher hand-copied with no parity test — the same family, mechanised
- `feedback_corrections_replace` in Claude memory — the prose version, which is why this exists

### #72 Onboard 3 men's leagues (full coverage) + evaluate 6 women's leagues (weak coverage); WSL not in provider catalog

_opened · created 2026-08-16_

Requested by the CPO, 2026-08-15. Research done, NOTHING onboarded — registry, dbt, and CI are
untouched. This is the handover for a fresh session using the `onboard-competition` skill.

## What was asked, and what already exists

| requested | state |
|---|---|
| Liga Portugal | ✅ already active — `LP`, 6 seasons, 2021-2026 |
| Eredivisie | ✅ already active — `ED`, 5 seasons, 2022-2026 |
| Belgian Pro League, Süper Lig, Ekstraklasa | ❌ not onboarded — see below |
| WSL, NWSL, Liga F, Frauen-Bundesliga, Première Ligue, Serie A Femminile, Liga MX Femenil | ❌ none onboarded, no women’s competition exists in the registry today |

## ⭐ THE DECISIVE FINDING: provider coverage is NOT uniform across these 9

Verified live against `/leagues` (id lookup, `api_coverage.fixtures.*` per current season) —
not assumed, not copied from the request. `stats_fix` / `stats_players` / `lineups` / `events`
are what the ingestion actually fanouts out to fetch; `False` across the board means fixtures
and standings only — no lineups, no fixture stats, no player stats, no match events. That is a
materially thinner product than every existing men’s top-flight league in the registry.

### Men’s — all 3 have FULL coverage, straightforward onboards

| League | Provider ID | Country | Seasons available | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Belgian Pro League (API name: "Jupiler Pro League") | 144 | Belgium | 17 (2010-2026) | ALL True |
| Süper Lig | 203 | Turkey | 16 (2011-2026) | ALL True |
| Ekstraklasa | 106 | Poland | 9 (2018-2026) | ALL True |

These look exactly like the existing domestic-league onboards (BL1/PL/PD pattern) — same
coverage profile as the leagues already active.

### Women’s — 6 of 7 found, coverage is WEAK on 5 of the 6

| Requested | API name found | Provider ID | Country | Seasons available | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| NWSL | "NWSL Women" | 254 | USA | 8 (2019-2026) | **ALL True** — the one full-coverage women’s league |
| Frauen-Bundesliga | "Frauen Bundesliga" | 82 | Germany | 11 (2016-2026) | ALL False |
| Serie A Femminile | "Serie A Women" | 139 | Italy | 11 (2016-2026) | ALL False |
| Liga F | "Primera División Femenina" (pre-rebrand API name) | 142 | Spain | 11 (2016-2026) | ALL False |
| Première Ligue | "Feminine Division 1" (D1 Arkema, pre-rebrand API name) | 64 | France | 14 (2013-2026) | ALL False |
| Liga MX Femenil | "Liga MX Femenil" | 673 | Mexico | 7 (2020-2026) | lineups+events True, stats False |
| **WSL (England)** | **NOT FOUND** | — | — | — | — |

**WSL is not in the provider catalog at all.** Searched exhaustively: "Women", "Women Super
League", "Women's Super League", "WSL", "WSL1", "Super League", "FA Women", "Women's Super",
"Barclays", "Championship". England's ONLY women’s competition in API-Football is "Women's
Championship" (id 699, tier 2) — the second division. **The competition asked for does not
exist on this provider.** Either drop it, or this needs a second provider for one league alone,
which is a bigger decision than onboarding.

## ⚠ CPO DECISIONS STILL OPEN — none of these are the builder’s to set

Per `docs/competition_registry.yml`'s own onboarding rules and `CLAUDE.md`: `history_seasons`
"Never increase without explicit approval in the same conversation" and needs a stated
rationale, and `ingest_active` must be set explicitly before any code is written.

1. **`history_seasons` per league.** The API ceiling is now known (table above) — that is NOT
   the answer, just the boundary. Existing domestic leagues use two depths on stated reasons:
   10-11 seasons for the "Big 5 parity" group (BL1 reference implementation), 5 seasons for
   leagues onboarded for WC-2026 squad-coverage reasons only. None of these 9 has a stated
   reason yet.
2. **Is thin coverage (5 of 6 women’s leagues) worth onboarding at all?** Fixtures + standings
   only, no player stats, no lineups, no events — every mart/metric that depends on those inputs
   would be empty for these leagues. This is a product-scope call, not a data one.
3. **WSL: drop, or pursue a second provider?** A second provider for one league is a NEW
   MECHANISM (§10) and needs its own decision, separate from this batch.
4. **Cost.** Each onboard is `ingest_active: true` from day one per the registry’s own rule — a
   recurring cost decision, sized differently depending on `history_seasons` chosen above.

## Two tooling notes for whoever picks this up

- `scripts/diagnostics/discover_competition.py --search ... --country X` — **the `--country`
  filter appears broken**: it returned zero results for exact, correctly-cased matches (e.g.
  `--search "Bundesliga" --country Germany` found nothing, while the same search with no
  country filter found it immediately, ID 78, country="Germany" exactly as printed). Search
  without `--country` and eyeball the country column instead until this is fixed.
- Several API names differ from common/brand names and will not turn up on an intuitive search:
  Liga F -> "Primera División Femenina", Première Ligue -> "Feminine Division 1", Belgian Pro
  League -> "Jupiler Pro League".

## Suggested next steps

1. Take items 1-4 above to the CPO as a single blinded decision (§11): which leagues, what
   depth, whether thin women’s coverage is acceptable, and what to do about WSL.
2. Once decided, `onboard-competition` skill per league — registry entry, `sync_dbt_vars.py`,
   i18n labels. Zero dbt file changes per the no-new-model rule.
3. Consider batching the 3 men’s leagues as one onboarding MR (same coverage profile, same
   pattern as existing leagues) and treating the women’s set as a separate decision entirely,
   since its product-scope question is materially different.

### #73 data:build:mr must not bootstrap-ingest (an unmerged branch writes prod raw; closes #33 item 13 for the MR path)

_closed · created 2026-08-16 · closed 2026-08-17_

## The problem, correctly stated

`data:build:mr` bootstrap-ingests any new `league_code` at MR time. That ingest writes
**PRODUCTION raw**: `ingestion/api_football/settings.py:31` defaults the raw dataset to `raw`, and
`API_FOOTBALL_BIGQUERY_DATASET` is set nowhere in `.gitlab-ci.yml`. So an unmerged feature branch
writes prod data.

This repo already knew that was wrong. `.gitlab-ci.yml:497`, verbatim:

> (That an MR pipeline can write prod raw AT ALL is a separate, still open question -- #33 item 13.)

It surfaced now only because GitLab refused to hand the key over: `API_FOOTBALL_API_KEY` is a
**protected** CI/CD variable, and protected variables are exposed only to pipelines on protected
branches. Only `main` is protected. So MR !50 (#72, onboarding BPL/TSL/EKS) died with:

```
ValueError: Missing API_FOOTBALL_API_KEY
```

**GitLab was doing the right thing.** It blocked an unmerged branch from writing production data.
Under GitHub Actions the same step "worked" because the secret was available to every branch --
the unsafe write succeeded silently instead of failing loudly. That is not a capability we lost;
it is a hole that got closed.

## The fix

**Delete the bootstrap-ingest step from `data:build:mr`.** It is redundant: `data:build:main:597`
already runs the identical `get_new_league_codes.py` + `python -m ingestion.api_football.main`
sequence, on `main`, which IS protected and DOES get the key. A newly onboarded league gets
ingested exactly once, post-merge, from the authoritative branch.

Three things this buys, beyond fixing the failure:
1. No unmerged branch can write prod raw (closes #33 item 13 for the MR path).
2. `data:build:mr` stops needing `API_FOOTBALL_API_KEY` at all -- the protected variable stays
   protected, and nothing is unprotected to work around it.
3. Drops a billed `SELECT DISTINCT league_code FROM RAW_APIF_FIXTURES_NEXT` from every MR
   pipeline, plus the API quota an unmerged branch would have burned.

No ingestion code changes. Onboarding a competition stays what it should be: a registry entry.

### The part that is NOT a simple deletion

`dbt_project/tests/assert_base_leagues_covers_active_competition_var.sql` (severity=error) fails
when a code is in `vars.active_competition_league_codes` but absent from `base_apif__leagues`. An
onboarding MR adds the code to the var; with bootstrap ingest gone, the raw rows do not exist
until after merge. **That test cannot pass at MR time for a league-adding MR, by construction.**

This is the same class as the ruling already recorded in `escalations.log`: *a change to seed
VALUES and a guard that depends on those values cannot land in the same PR -- the values merge
first, then the guard.*

The invariant it asserts -- "the warehouse covers every active competition" -- is a **prod**
invariant. It should be asserted where it can hold: on `data:build:main` and `data:nightly`, both
of which run `--target prod` AFTER the bootstrap ingest. Proposed: tag the test and exclude it
from `data:build:mr`'s dbt invocations ONLY. It keeps running on main and nightly, unchanged.

Per the repo's standing rule this is a NARROWING, not a loosening -- the assertion still runs
everywhere it is answerable. Stated plainly so it can be attacked in review:

> **Consequence:** a newly onboarded league is not validated by this test until after merge. If
> its post-merge ingest fails, `data:build:main` goes red. That is the correct place for it to go
> red -- main is where prod state is asserted -- but it does mean an onboarding MR can merge green
> and break main. The alternative is an unmerged branch writing prod raw, which is worse.

## Rejected: unprotecting API_FOOTBALL_API_KEY

The original version of this issue listed "unprotect the variable" as a co-equal option. It was
not one, and it has been removed rather than left on the page. It exposes a live API key to every
branch to buy a step that should not run on a branch at all. CPO 2026-08-16: *"it is 100%
bullshit in terms of security."* Correct.

Refs: #33 item 13, #72, !50

### #74 The nightly's Cloud Run image never tracks main, so prod silently reverts every merged change at 04:00

_opened · created 2026-08-16 · labels: bug_

The nightly runs a Cloud Run image built by hand with `gcloud run jobs deploy --source .`. That
command packages **the working tree at that moment**. Nothing rebuilds it when `main` moves, so the
image is a frozen copy of the repo and prod silently runs old code.

## Measured, 2026-08-16

```
running image      fdp-nightly@sha256:2fa6a5fd…      built 2026-08-14 13:14 UTC
!43 (country fix)  merged                                   2026-08-15
entrypoint.sh      dbt build --target prod                  no selector — EVERY node
last execution     2026-08-16 04:00                         succeeded
staging table      last modified 2026-08-16 04:52           rebuilt by that run
```

Result, with `main` carrying the fix and prod not:

```
main  stg_apif__leagues.sql   json_value(row_json, '$.country.name')
prod  staging.stg_apif__leagues   country non-null        0 / 467
prod  core.dim_league             league_country non-null   0 / 45
```

`data:build:main` had already run green on `!43`'s and `!45`'s merges and written the correct
values. The nightly then rebuilt the entire warehouse from 14 August code and reverted them.

**So the nightly does not just fail to apply merged changes — it actively undoes them**, every night,
for every model. `!43` and `!45` are the instance; the mechanism applies to any dbt or ingestion
change.

## Why nothing caught it

- **The job reports success.** It runs fine; it just runs old code. Execution status carries no
  information about which commit is inside the container, so every alert and every dashboard is
  green while prod drifts.
- **`deploy/nightly/README.md` presents the deploy under "One-time setup".** It reads like
  infrastructure you provision once. It is actually a build step that must re-run on every change,
  and nothing in the doc says so.
- **There is no deploy step anywhere.** Verified 2026-08-16: `gcloud builds triggers list` returns
  nothing in any region, and no job in `.gitlab-ci.yml` references `fdp-nightly`. The newest image
  in the registry before today was 2026-08-14 — nothing had rebuilt it in two days.

## The fix is not "remember to redeploy"

That is the same class as every other prose-only rule this repo has watched fail. The image must
track `main` by machinery. Shapes worth weighing, none chosen here:

1. **A GitLab CI job on `main`** that runs `gcloud run jobs deploy` when the paths baked into the
   image change. ⚠ `.gitlab-ci.yml` is a PROTECTED path, so this is a governance task with
   `protected_override`, and it adds a recurring build cost — CPO-class on both counts.
2. **A Cloud Build trigger** on push to `main`. Moves the mechanism out of the repo, which is
   exactly what #39 wanted for the nightly itself, but it is then invisible to code review.
3. **Make staleness VISIBLE rather than impossible** — the job logs the commit SHA it was built
   from, and something compares it to `main`. Cheaper, and it converts a silent revert into a
   noisy one. Does not stop the revert.

⚠ Whatever is chosen, it must cover **ingestion code too**, not only dbt models. The image carries
the whole repo, so a stale image reverts ingestion behaviour with equal silence.

## Immediate state

The image was redeployed by hand on 2026-08-16 14:34 (`sha256:584209e0`), so tonight's run carries
the country fix. ⚠ **Prod is still wrong until a build actually runs.** The nightly exits 0 without
building when ingestion reports `new_data=false`, so a quiet night will not repair it; a merge
touching `.data_paths_prod` would, via `data:build:main`.

## Related

- **#39** moved the nightly to Cloud Run — this defect arrived with that move and is not an argument
  against it. Running in CI had worse failure modes.
- **#4** a web dispatch from any branch builds prod from THAT branch's code — the same class of
  defect, where what runs is not what `main` says.
- **#30** finding: of 50 corrections, 33 were prose-only and 22 recurred. Every rule that got a
  mechanism stopped. A README sentence saying "re-run this after every change" is the losing option.

### #75 Fixture-event integrity failures are what turn the nightly red, and one bad row skips 103-540 nodes

_opened · created 2026-08-16 · labels: bug_

The nightly's red nights are **data quality in fixture events**, not infrastructure. A single
referential-integrity failure fails the run and dbt skips everything downstream of it, so a one-row
defect stops a large part of the warehouse from being written.

## Measured

**2026-08-16** (execution `fdp-nightly-gcl29`):

```
Done. PASS=899  WARN=1  ERROR=1  SKIP=103  TOTAL=1004
Failure: relationships_fct_fixture_event_player_sk__player_sk__ref_dim_player_
```

The offending data is **one row**:

```
player_sk   league_code   rows
544602      CIT           1
```

One event in Coppa Italia references a player id that is not in `dim_player`. That single row
skipped **103 nodes**.

**2026-08-12** (execution `fdp-nightly-rtr5d`) failed on a *different* test in the same area:

```
Done. PASS=428  WARN=1  ERROR=1  SKIP=540  TOTAL=970
Failure: assert_event_team_in_fixture_participants
```

That one skipped **540 nodes** — more than half the warehouse.

So across the two failures we can inspect, both are fixture-event integrity, and both are
single-assertion failures with very large blast radii.

## What this is NOT

⚠ **Not the gate misbehaving.** `dbt build` marks dependents of a failed test as skipped
deliberately, so prod keeps its last good data rather than being overwritten with output built on
top of a known-bad row. `.gitlab-ci.yml` documents that choice at length. The gate is correct; the
data underneath it is not.

⚠ **Not #74.** That issue is about the nightly running a stale image. This is about the nightly
failing while running the *right* code. They are independent and both were live at once, which is
why the country fix took two days to reach prod.

## Why it matters more than one row suggests

A referential failure anywhere in fixture events can skip a majority of the build, so the cost is
set by the blast radius, not by the size of the defect. On 08-12 that was 540 nodes for one
assertion. And because the same failure recurs on different tests on different nights, the effect
is an intermittently stale warehouse with a green-looking job history — the nightly reports failure,
but nothing reads that failure and connects it to "the site's data did not update".

## Work

1. **Identify the orphan.** `player_sk` 544602 in CIT: is the player genuinely absent from the
   provider's `/players` responses for that season, or is it a coverage gap in what we ingest?
   `dim_player` is built from the player universe; an event can reference a player who never
   appeared in a squad or profile pull.
2. **Decide the treatment.** Options not chosen here: ingest the missing player, exclude events
   whose player is unknown, or downgrade the test to `warn` for this specific class. ⚠ The third is
   the one to be careful with — the "never loosen a guard" rule applies, and a `warn` here would
   trade a visible failure for a silent one.
3. **Do the same for `assert_event_team_in_fixture_participants`**, which is a separate root cause
   with the larger blast radius.
4. **Consider whether a one-row integrity defect SHOULD stop 103–540 nodes.** It currently does, by
   design. That design is defensible, but it means the product's freshness is one bad provider row
   away from stopping, with no alert that says so in those terms.

## Related

- **#74** the nightly's image never tracks `main` — the other reason prod drifts.
- **#33 item 14** the deliberate 7-day re-fetch skip, which is what the completeness gate misread
  earlier; unrelated to this, but the same "nightly went red" symptom.

### #76 Record whether a competition has been INGESTED, not only that it should be (one missing fact behind 3 symptoms)

_opened · created 2026-08-16_

## One missing fact, three symptoms

`docs/competition_registry.yml` records that a competition **should** be ingested (`status`,
`ingest_active`). **Nothing records whether it has been.** That single absence causes all three of
the following, and each has been worked around separately rather than fixed at the source.

### Symptom 1: DQ tests cannot ask the right question

Four singular tests assert *"every code in `vars.active_competition_league_codes` has rows"*:

- `assert_base_leagues_covers_active_competition_var`
- `assert_base_teams_covers_active_competition_var`
- `assert_base_fixtures_next_covers_active_competition_var`
- `assert_fct_fixture_covers_active_competition_var`

All four are unconditional (`left join ... where null`). On an MR that onboards a competition they
fail by construction: the MR adds the code, and since !53 the MR pipeline no longer ingests, so the
rows cannot exist until post-merge.

The question they ask is *"does this league have data?"*. The question they should ask is
**"should this league have data yet?"**. They cannot ask it, because the answer is not recorded
anywhere.

(The other four `*_covers_active_competition_var` tests -- standings, fixture_statistics,
fct_standings, fct_fixture_team_stats -- happen not to fail, because they `inner join
base_apif__leagues` on a coverage flag and a league with no rows silently drops out of "required".
That is luck, not design, and it is its own small hazard: the gate is degenerate exactly when the
league is missing.)

### Symptom 2: a billed query per run to rediscover it

`scripts/get_new_league_codes.py` exists solely to reconstruct this fact. Every `data:build:main`
run executes `SELECT DISTINCT league_code FROM RAW_APIF_FIXTURES_NEXT` to work out which leagues
are new. The system pays BigQuery to rediscover something it should already know.

### Symptom 3: a special path for onboarding

Because "new league" is not a state the system holds, it needs a distinct **bootstrap** code path
(`API_FOOTBALL_LEAGUE_CODES=<new> API_FOOTBALL_INCLUDE_IN_PROGRESS=1`) separate from the normal
run. A new league is not special. It is a league with no data yet. Two paths for one job is where
drift comes from, and it is the direct reason #73 existed at all.

## What to design

Not proposed as a solution, deliberately -- the design is the work:

- What exactly gets recorded (per league? per league+entity? per league+entity+season?)
- Where it lives (a BigQuery table written by the loaders, a dbt snapshot, something else)
- Who writes it and when (each loader on success? the orchestrator at the end of a phase?)
- How the DQ tests consume it so they answer correctly at MR time AND on prod, with no skipping
  and no exclusion list
- Whether it subsumes `get_new_league_codes.py` entirely
- Whether the bootstrap path can then be deleted, so onboarding uses the ordinary run

## Why file it rather than patch around it

CPO ruling 2026-08-16, on being asked whether !53 was a systematic fix or a hack: **"ship part 1
and file the state fix as its own issue."**

The alternative already got built and rejected. Tagging one DQ test `prod_state` and excluding it
from the MR job was failed by all four routed reviewers as a coverage cut, and the scope claim
behind it was wrong (it said one test was affected; four are). Full record in
`.claude/task/escalations.log`, entry 2026-08-16.

⚠ Until this lands, an MR that onboards a competition shows RED on those four tests and is merged
on judgement. That is accepted and documented in `.gitlab-ci.yml` at the `dbt test` step of
`data:build:mr`. **Do not silence the tests to make it green.**

## Related

- !53 / #73 -- removed the MR-time ingest, which is what exposed this
- #33 item 13 -- MR pipelines writing prod raw; closed for the MR path by !53, broader question open
- #72 / !50 -- the onboarding MR that ran into all of it

### #77 Task artifacts serialise the repo: split per-task paperwork from durable records

_opened · created 2026-08-17_

## The defect

Per-task state is stored as **committed files at fixed paths**:

    .claude/task/contract.md
    .claude/task/review.md
    .claude/task/review_input.patch

One path, one task. Two branches each write their own — fine while working — and then **both merge
to main**, so main carries whichever landed last and the next branch inherits a contract describing
someone else's task. The governance model is single-task-per-repo by construction, and that is what
makes parallel branches collide.

Real teams do not hit this because per-task paperwork never lands on the trunk: the MR carries the
review, main carries the code.

## Evidence, all from 2026-08-17

Four collisions in one day, every one of them an artifact conflict and none of them a code conflict:

- `!57` conflicted on `active_work.md` + `escalations.log`
- `!62` conflicted on `contract.md` + `review.md` + `review_input.patch`
- `active_work.md`'s top section was rewritten by the product stream, so the pipeline worktree's
  handover pointed at the competitions page — the exact re-scope the file's own header forbids
- Two contracts existed simultaneously, each describing a different task, with the gates reading
  whichever happened to be checked out

⛔ Two answers were considered and REJECTED; do not revisit them:
- **Serialize / drop the second worktree.** Accepts the broken constraint instead of fixing it, and
  costs parallel work outright.
- **Give each worktree its own handover.** Fixes one of the four collisions and leaves the worst
  one (`contract.md`) untouched.

## The fix: two kinds of file, currently treated the same

**A. Per-task paperwork — `contract.md`, `review.md`, `review_input.patch`.**
Needed ON THE BRANCH so CI can check them. **Not needed on main.** If they do not persist on main,
two branches can never collide, because each starts from nothing. This alone kills the `!62` class.

**B. Durable records — `escalations.log`, `active_work.md`.**
These genuinely belong on main.
- `escalations.log` is **append-only**, so it is a solved problem: `merge=union` in `.gitattributes`
  makes those conflicts vanish mechanically instead of by hand.
- `active_work.md` is a living document and the only genuinely hard case. It needs one owner or
  explicit per-stream sections. **CPO decision, not an implementation choice.**

## Scope and traps

Protected paths → `protected_override` + non-placeholder impact_map + **cto-reviewer and
platform-reviewer at OPUS**. Consumers to trace before changing anything:

- `.claude/review_routing.json` — `artifact_only`, `artifact_only_never`, `hash_exclude_paths`,
  `review_exclude_paths` all name these files literally
- `scripts/check_task_artifacts.py` — runs in `validate:governance`, recomputes `diff_sha256` from
  `git diff base...HEAD`. ⚠ Whatever changes, the CI binding must still work: the review must stay
  provably tied to the MR's code (F11/#409).
- `.claude/hooks/git_discipline.py` — the commit gate reads `review.md`, computes `--staged-hash`,
  and enforces required reviewers per staged path
- `.claude/hooks/task_contract_gate.py` — reads `contract.md` for `scope_paths`
- `docs/working_agreement.md` §2 — describes all of this in prose and must move with it
- `tests/` — `test_every_task_artifact_is_classified` fails when a file appears in `.claude/task/`
  that is neither excluded nor one of the two authority files

⚠ **The gates do not understand a merge** (already logged, `active_work.md` OWED): mid-merge they
call what the other branch brings in "out of scope" and recommend `git checkout -- <file>`, which
DELETES it. Any change here should fix that too — a `MERGE_HEAD`-aware skip — since it is the same
root cause: machinery that assumes one linear task.

## Why it matters

CPO, 2026-08-17: 12 MRs in one day, only 5 product, 7 paperwork about the product. *"With this speed
the website will never get done."* This issue is the structural half of that: the paperwork is not
just verbose, it is serialising the work.

- docs/metrics_context_model.md:12
- docs/north_star.md:108
- docs/site_architecture.md:34

### #81 Nothing collapses two provider records for the same club, so a duplicate keeps its own name and its own URL

_opened · created 2026-08-20_

Where API-Football holds two team ids for one real club, the pipeline has no mechanism to fold them. Both records survive with their own name and their own URL.

team_name_overrides is not that mechanism: it corrects a DISPLAY NAME on one team_api_id. fixture_event_team_overrides is not either - it is ref()d only by base_apif__fixture_events, so its alias mode corrects event attribution and nothing in the team-identity chain reads it. An alias row there folds no team, removes no URL and changes no slug.
